name: On-Chain Forensics
title: On-Chain Forensics
answer: On-chain forensics is the practice of tracing crypto transactions across public blockchains to identify the parties involved and the flow of funds. It covers Bitcoin, Ethereum, stablecoins, DeFi protocols, bridges, and mixers, and it supports investigations into hacks, ransomware, scams, sanctions evasion, and market manipulation. The work serves exchanges, law enforcement, compliance teams, and journalists who need to understand who moved what and when. It overlaps with blockchain analytics but places more emphasis on investigative narrative and attribution than on raw data dashboards.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: On-chain forensics is the practice of tracing crypto transactions across public blockchains to identify the parties involved and the flow of funds. It covers Bitcoin, Ethereum, stablecoins, DeFi protocols, bridges, and mixers, and it supports investigations into hacks, ransomware, scams, sanctions evasion, and market manipulation. The work serves exchanges, law enforcement, compliance teams, and journalists who need to understand who moved what and when. It overlaps with blockchain analytics but places more emphasis on investigative narrative and attribution than on raw data dashboards.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on full nodes and archive nodes that hold complete transaction histories, plus indexers that make queries fast. Commercial platforms such as Chainalysis, Elliptic, and TRM Labs provide address labels, risk scores, and investigation interfaces, while open tools like Nansen, Dune Analytics, and Glassnode offer query and dashboard layers. Behind these interfaces sit graph databases, cloud compute, and APIs that connect wallet addresses to entities and clusters. Machine learning models help with clustering and anomaly detection, but the underlying data is still the public ledger itself.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Investigators combine heuristics with manual review, starting from common input ownership, change address detection, and address reuse to group addresses into likely wallets. They then follow transaction graphs across chains, using bridge and exchange deposit data to link on-chain activity to real-world identities. Clustering algorithms and machine learning can flag patterns such as coinjoin use, peel chains, or rapid layering, but analysts verify each lead against labels and off-chain records. Open-source intelligence, subpoenas, and exchange cooperation often fill the gaps that the ledger alone cannot resolve.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk are central because on-chain forensics can expose personal financial data and because labels and heuristics can be wrong. The site's 215 compliance and regulation pages cover the rules that shape this work, including anti-money laundering, sanctions screening, and the travel rule. Provenance matters: a label may come from an exchange, a law enforcement notice, or a heuristic, and each source carries different reliability and legal weight. False positives can freeze funds or damage reputations, so investigators document their methods and keep a clear chain of custody for any evidence.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward cross-chain and layer 2 coverage, where assets move through bridges and rollups that fragment the transaction graph. Privacy tools such as zero-knowledge proofs and mixers will keep raising the cost of attribution, while AI-generated scams and deepfake social engineering add new investigation targets. Regulators are pushing for real-time monitoring and more formal reporting, which pulls on-chain forensics closer to traditional financial compliance. The likely direction is more automation in clustering and alerting, paired with human analysts who can explain and defend the findings.
